records.title: [FEATURE]: Ordered cross-pipeline deploy/run from control lineage (package phase)
records.body:
## TL;DR

flowx emits **one DAB per ADF pipeline** with **no notion of ordering** across them. When one pipeline calls another via `ExecutePipeline`, the generated `run_job_task` points at a job living in a *sibling* bundle — so `bundle deploy` breaks, and today's fix (FLOWX-7) only patches it with a manual `${var.X}` placeholder the operator fills in by hand. That's deploy-valid but **records no ordering**, and is wired one-bundle-at-a-time with no global view of the call graph.

This is the **"2b" follow-up #23 deferred**: consume #23's deterministic `lineage.control_edges` in the **package phase** to emit real, ordered cross-pipeline references. Recommended: **generate a top-level orchestration bundle** (Option B) whose `run_job_task` DAG encodes `depends_on` straight from the control graph, plus **deploy-ordering** (Option C) so callee bundles register before callers. **Depends on #23.**

---

## The gap

Verified against source — four facts:

1. **One bundle per pipeline.** `dab_writer.main` writes each workflow to its own dir and calls `write_bundle` per workflow (`dab_writer.py:434-447`); each emits an independent `databricks.yml` + `resources/*.yml` (`:81-159`). Documented in the package skill (`flowx-package/SKILL.md:247`). This is FLOWX-7 (`KNOWN_ISSUES_RCA.md:142-160`).
2. **`ExecutePipeline` → a cross-bundle `run_job_task`.** `execute_pipeline.prepare` lowers the call to `run_job_task.job_id = ${resources.jobs.<callee>.id}` (`execute_pipeline.py:49-52`). That reference only resolves inside *this* bundle, but the callee lives in a sibling bundle → `bundle deploy` fails with `no such node "resources.jobs.X"`.
3. **The FLOWX-7 fix is deploy-valid but not ordered.** `_rewrite_cross_bundle_run_job_refs` rewrites the unresolved ref to `${var.X}` (`dab_writer.py:1209-1248`) and surfaces a manual SETUP.md row telling the operator to pass `--var "X=<job_id>"` (`prereqs_writer.py:509-525`). It **records no deploy/run ordering**, works one bundle at a time (`_cross_bundle_variables` resets per `write_bundle`), and leaves an exactly-knowable relationship to be reconstructed by hand.
4. **No ordering logic exists anywhere.** Nothing orders bundles, generates an orchestration job, or sequences deploys; `main` simply loops workflows in report order.

**What #23 gives us.** #23 adds a deterministic `lineage` block to `inventory.json` with `control_edges` (caller→callee `ExecutePipeline` edges: `caller_pipeline`, `callee_pipeline`, `activity_name`, `wait_on_completion`). That's the global input this issue needs — it names, before packaging runs, exactly which callee bundles each caller depends on. **This issue consumes it.**

---

## Proposed solution

Consume `control_edges` in the package layer to replace manual `${var.X}` wiring with real, ordered references. Repo conventions (`AGENTS.md`): `@dataclass(slots=True, kw_only=True)` models, deterministic bundler logic, golden-file tests.

**Option B — top-level orchestration bundle (RECOMMENDED).** Emit one additional generated bundle with a single orchestration job: one `run_job_task` per migrated pipeline, `depends_on` derived directly from `control_edges` (caller depends on callee, honoring `wait_on_completion`). A single deployable artifact expressing the whole call graph as a real Databricks Jobs DAG — a shape the codebase already models (`RunJobActivity` `ir.py:328-340`; the `parent_child_orchestration` motif `motifs.py:120-131`). It captures ordering **as data the platform enforces**, needs no per-bundle rewrite gymnastics, and composes with the existing per-pipeline bundles (still the deploy unit for the child jobs).

**Option C — ordered deploys (COMPANION).** Topologically sort the per-pipeline bundles from `control_edges` so callees deploy/register before callers, and emit the ordered `databricks bundle deploy` sequence into SETUP.md. Cheap; ship alongside B so the numeric job IDs a caller needs exist by deploy time.

**Option A — real cross-bundle `run_job_task` wiring (rejected).** Replace `${var.X}` with the callee's real reference. Weakest: DAB `${resources.jobs.X.id}` only resolves within one bundle, so a genuine symbolic cross-bundle reference isn't confirmable (see open questions), and without a shared bundle it degrades to the same manual numeric ID — the same step, relocated.

**Recommendation: B (primary) + C (companion).** B produces the enforceable ordering artifact; C ensures the underlying per-pipeline bundles register in dependency order.

**Cycle handling.** ADF permits A→B and B→A; a Jobs DAG cannot be cyclic. The builder must detect cycles (deterministic DFS/SCC) and, on detection, break the back-edge, emit the tasks without the offending `depends_on`, and record a WARNINGS.md/SETUP.md note naming the cycle members so the operator decides the real ordering. Never emit an invalid DAG.

---

## Touch points

- **New consumer** — read `inventory.json`'s `lineage.control_edges` (#23) and build a caller→callee graph keyed by `normalize_task_key(pipeline_name)` to align with the resource keys `execute_pipeline.prepare` already emits (`execute_pipeline.py:49`).
- **`dab_writer.py`** — new `write_orchestration_bundle`, invoked from `main` (`:434-459`) after the per-pipeline bundles, reusing `_build_databricks_yml` (`:576`) and the `run_job_task` shape. Deploy-ordering (C) is computed here from the same graph.
- **`prereqs_writer.py`** — when the orchestration job resolves a caller's edge, drop/downgrade the manual "Cross-bundle job references" SETUP.md row (`:509-525`); keep it as the fallback for unresolved callees (partial exports).

**FLOWX-7 interaction.** The `${var.X}` placeholder stays as the backward-compatible fallback for callees absent from the current export or when the orchestration bundle is disabled. When #23's graph resolves a callee, the orchestration job's `depends_on` becomes the source of ordering truth and the placeholder becomes a safety net, not the primary mechanism.

---

## Testing

Repo conventio

records.title: Implement init, add_edge, traverse and deinit in specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27
records.body:
## Context

`specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27` is the breadth-first traversal of the Trinity
graph library, sitting beside `graph.t27`, `graph_dfs.t27`, `dijkstra.t27`,
`bellman_ford.t27`, `prims_mst.t27`, `topological_sort.t27` and
`disjoint_set.t27` in `specs/tri/graph/`. It owns two types: a `Graph` holding
an adjacency list `adj : [][]usize` indexed by vertex id plus the allocator that
made it, and a `BFSResult` holding two parallel arrays — `order` (the visit
sequence) and `distance` (hops from the source) — plus its own allocator. The
module's six test blocks already spell out the properties the structures must
have: one adjacency row per vertex, an undirected edge written into both
endpoints' rows, the handshake lemma (degree sum equals twice the edge count),
an isolated vertex keeping a length-0 row, `order.len == distance.len` with the
source at distance 0, and BFS distances rising by at most 1 along the visit
order. All four functions are empty bodies, so none of it is produced by code
yet. Your job is to write those four bodies.

`.t27` is hand-authored source, compiled out to C/Rust/Verilog/Zig by `t27c`.
You are writing the input language.

## Exact current state

All commands run from `/Users/playom/t27`.

```
$ ./target/release/t27c parse specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27 2>&1 | grep -E '^(recovery-events|declarations-swallowed|lexer-discarded-chars):'
recovery-events: 0
declarations-swallowed: 0
lexer-discarded-chars: 0
```

```
$ ./target/release/t27c count specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27 | head -1
graph_bfs.t27: 7 node types
```

```
$ grep -c 'TODO: Implement' specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27
4
```

```
$ grep -cE '^[[:space:]]*test ' specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27
6
```

The file parses clean today. Keep it clean, and keep all six existing test
blocks exactly as they are — they are the specification.

## What to write

Four functions. Signatures quoted verbatim — change only the bodies.

1. `fn init(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, vertex_count: usize) -> Graph`
   Allocate `adj` with exactly `vertex_count` rows, each an empty slice, and
   store the allocator in the struct. One row per vertex even when a vertex has
   no neighbours — that is `test adjacency_has_one_row_per_vertex` and
   `test an_isolated_vertex_has_an_empty_row`.

2. `fn add_edge(graph: *Graph, from: usize, to: usize) -> void`
   Undirected: append `to` to `graph.adj[from]` **and** `from` to
   `graph.adj[to]`, growing both rows through `graph.allocator`. Writing only
   one direction breaks both
   `test an_undirected_edge_appears_in_both_endpoints_rows` and
   `test the_degree_sum_is_twice_the_edge_count`.

3. `fn traverse(graph: *Graph, start: usize, allocator: std.mem.Allocator) -> BFSResult`
   Standard BFS with an explicit FIFO queue and a visited marker. Allocate
   `order` and `distance` from the `allocator` argument (not the graph's), set
   `distance[start] = 0`, and push neighbours in adjacency-row order so the
   result is deterministic. Return a `BFSResult` whose `order` and `distance`
   are the same length and whose `allocator` field is the one passed in — that
   pair of facts is `test bfs_result_holds_one_distance_per_vertex_and_starts_at_zero`.
   Because BFS explores by layer, the distance must rise by at most 1 between
   consecutive entries of `order`, which is
   `test bfs_distances_never_jump_by_more_than_one`.

4. `fn deinit(graph: *Graph) -> void`
   Free every adjacency row and then the row array itself, through
   `graph.allocator`. This is the file's own header comment: "Free graph
   memory". `BFSResult` carries its own allocator for the caller to free
   separately; note that in a comment.

### The tests are the specification

One of the six, quoted verbatim, to show the style the file uses:

```
    test the_degree_sum_is_twice_the_edge_count
        // Verify: the handshake lemma on the path 0 - 1 - 2 — two edges, so the
        // row lengths add up to four
        given row0 = [_]usize{ 1 }
        and row1 = [_]usize{ 0, 2 }
        and row2 = [_]usize{ 1 }
        and rows = [_][]usize{ @constCast(&row0), @constCast(&row1), @constCast(&row2) }
        when graph = Graph{ .adj = @constCast(&rows), .allocator = std.testing.allocator }
        and degree_sum = graph.adj[0].len + graph.adj[1].len + graph.adj[2].len
        then degree_sum == 4
```

Every existing test builds its graph by hand because no constructor worked. Add
at least one new `test` block per implemented function that goes through the
functions instead: `init(alloc, 3).adj.len == 3`; the path 0-1-2 built by two
`add_edge` calls reproducing the same both-rows shape; `traverse` on that path
from vertex 0 giving `order.len == distance.len` and `distance[0] == 0`; and a
`deinit` block stating the ownership rule. Do not delete or rewrite the six
existing blocks.

**There is no t27 interpreter.** Test blocks are parsed and counted, never
executed. Do not claim a test passed.

## Acceptance criteria

**Every criterion below is a command with an expected output, and every one of them
fails on the file as it stands today.** The `now` column was produced by running the
command in this repository on 2026-09-09. Re-run them before you start; you will get
the same numbers, and that is the point — a criterion that already passes before any
work is done proves nothing.

- 1. all 4 named functions still exist, every function body is non-empty, and `t27c parse` reports recovery-events 0, declarations-swallowed 0, lexer-discarded-chars 0
- 2. `grep -c 'TODO: Implement' specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27` prints 0
- 3. the real-code node count is at least 8
- 4. `t27c parse specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27 | grep -c 'kind: TestBlock'` prints at least 10
- 5. `t27c count specs/tri/graph/graph_bfs.t27 | head -1` reports at least 11 node types

| # | check | now (before you start) | required when you are done |
|---|-------|------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 | signatures + non-empty bodies + parse | `4 names, fns=4 nonem

records.title: Phase B: Federation read-path evolution for graph traversal
records.body:
## Context

Phase A (PR #9) ships bounded graph traversal via PostgreSQL recursive CTEs: neighborhood, shortest-path, and direction filters. All reads go through PG — no TerminusDB dependency.

Phase B extends the read path for federation and scale scenarios.

## Potential scope

- **TerminusDB read path**: Option to route traversal queries through TDB WOQL when TDB is available (PG remains fallback). Requires `graph_queries.py` backend abstraction — the current structure is designed for this swap.
- **Cross-node traversal**: Follow relationships that span federation peers (requires KOI-net protocol extensions for graph queries).
- **Materialized neighbor cache**: For high-fanout hub entities, pre-compute neighborhood at write time to avoid CTE cost at read time.
- **Graph analytics endpoints**: Degree distribution, connected components, centrality metrics — useful for understanding graph topology.
- **Pagination on neighborhood**: Current approach returns all nodes up to cap. For large neighborhoods, cursor-based pagination may be needed.

## Dependencies

- Phase 1 TerminusDB integration (smoke-validated, PR merged)
- Phase A graph traversal (PR #9)
- KOI-net federation stack (in progress on `feature/personal-koi-federation`)

## Not in scope

- Schema migrations (Phase A confirmed all required indexes exist)
- Auth model changes (localhost + WireGuard mesh is sufficient for personal KOI)

records.title: Create task graph algorithms module
records.body:
> **🎟️ PyCon 2026 Sprint Issue** — Reserved for the [PyCon 2026 sprint](https://github.com/lwgray/marcus/blob/develop/docs/sprints/pycon-2026.md) (May 2026 · Long Beach, CA). **At the sprint?** Comment below to claim it. **Working outside the sprint?** Please check in first — sprint participants get first pick.

---

## Background

**What is Marcus?**
Marcus is a system that coordinates multiple AI agents (Claude, GPT-4, etc.) to work on software projects in parallel. Think of it like a project manager: Marcus breaks a project into tasks, assigns them to AI workers, and tracks progress on a shared kanban board.

**What is a task graph?**
Marcus manages tasks that depend on each other — "write tests" can't happen before "implement feature". This forms a directed graph: nodes are tasks, edges are dependencies. Graph algorithms like cycle detection, topological sort, and critical path analysis are fundamental to Marcus's coordination logic.

---

## The Problem

The same graph algorithms are duplicated across 9 separate places in the codebase. Cycle detection alone appears in `task_execution_order.py`, `task_graph_validator.py`, `dependency_inferer.py` (4 times), `board_health.py`, `scheduler.py` (2 times), and `dependency_wiring.py` (2 times). When a bug is found in cycle detection, it must be fixed in 9 places.

**Relevant files:**
- `src/core/task_execution_order.py`
- `src/core/task_graph_validator.py`
- `src/core/dependency_inferer.py`
- `src/core/board_health.py`
- `src/core/scheduler.py`
- `src/core/dependency_wiring.py`

---

## Why it matters

Duplicated logic means bugs get fixed in some places but not others. It also makes new graph features (parallel scheduling, bottleneck detection) harder to add correctly. A single well-tested graph module makes the codebase easier to maintain and extend.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A new `src/core/graph/` module exists that consolidates graph algorithms (cycle detection, topological sort, critical path, DFS/BFS)
- [ ] At least 3 of the 9 existing duplicate implementations are replaced with calls to the new module
- [ ] The behavior of replaced code is unchanged — the same results are produced as before
- [ ] Every public function in the new module is covered by at least one automated test
- [ ] `topological_sort` on a 1000-node graph completes in under 100ms
- [ ] All existing tests still pass

---

## Getting help

- Comment on this issue — maintainers check frequently during the sprint
- See the [sprint menu](https://github.com/lwgray/marcus/blob/develop/docs/sprints/pycon-2026.md) for project overview
- Ask in the sprint room

records.title: Documentation of ast.walk misleadingly characterizes its behavior as recursive when it's really iterative
records.body:
# Documentation

Although the [documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ast.html#ast.walk) claims that `ast.walk` generates nodes "in no specified order" and even describes its behavior as "*Recursively* yield all descendant nodes...", a look at the [source code](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/fe85a8291d9aa11c9ce9e207c39ea0a0c35f9625/Lib/ast.py#L395) reveals that it really performs a breadth-first traversal by iteratively yielding child nodes in a queue:
```python
def walk(node):
    """
    Recursively yield all descendant nodes in the tree starting at *node*
    (including *node* itself), in no specified order.  This is useful if you
    only want to modify nodes in place and don't care about the context.
    """
    from collections import deque
    todo = deque([node])
    while todo:
        node = todo.popleft()
        todo.extend(iter_child_nodes(node))
        yield node
```
I thought that maybe this function used to be recursive but found that it has not been modified since its first appearance in CPython 2.6.3.

I think we should at the minimum remove the wording "Recursively" from the description, and optionally:
1. Clarify the actual ordering by changing "in no specified order" to "in breadth-first order".
2. Add a keyword argument such as `depth_first` that defaults to `False` such that when it is true, switches to a depth-first traversal that behaves like:
```python
def dfs_walk(node):
    yield node
    for child in ast.iter_child_nodes(node):
        yield from dfs_walk(child)
```

records.title: Perf ratchet for the sidebar collections tree
records.body:
## Context

#505 renders the album tree as one flat list derived from `albums()` on every listing change, with a recursive CTE per folder for counts and a full depth-first re-derivation on reorder. That is fine at tens of collections; it has no measured bound at hundreds or with deep nesting (six levels).

## Scope

- Add a perf-harness scenario (`tests/perf`) that seeds a library with a few hundred collections across the full depth bound and measures `album:list`, `album:reorder`, and `album:move` latency plus sidebar render time.
- Record the baseline and add it to the existing perf ratchet so regressions fail CI.
- If the recursive folder-count CTE dominates, materialize descendant counts or compute them once per listing rather than per folder.

Follow-up from #505.

records.title: comments: the depth-cap fallback can build the exact shape migration 0055's trigger aborts
records.body:
Found while checking that 0055 was safe to apply to the production D1. It was safe, and it is applied — `GET /api/official` now reads `triggers_missing: []`. This is about a path that is unreachable today and would fail loudly rather than quietly if it ever stopped being.

`createComment` in `src/society.ts` sets both values in one branch:

```
storedParentId = anchor ? anchor.id : null;
depth = anchor ? anchor.depth + 1 : 0;
intendedParentId = parentId;
```

`intendedParentId` is assigned unconditionally. `storedParentId` is assigned unconditionally too — but to `null` when the walk found no ancestor, and that null is the whole defect. So `anchor === null` yields `parent_id IS NULL` with `intended_parent_id` set — precisely the shape `comments_intended_parent_needs_parent_insert` raises `ABORT` on.

Before 0055 that combination was a graceful degradation: the reply landed at top level, the intent was still recorded, and the citizen got their comment. After 0055 the insert aborts, and the citizen gets a failed write instead.

**Why it does not fire today.** The recursive CTE walks up from `parentId` selecting rows with `depth < max_comment_depth`, and the root of any chain is depth 0, so a qualifying ancestor always exists. The code says so itself: *"An ancestor at depth < cap always exists (the root is depth 0), but if the walk somehow finds none, fall back to top level rather than guess."* Production currently holds zero rows in the contradictory shape.

**Why it is still worth fixing.** The fallback exists because someone thought the walk could return nothing — a broken parent chain, or a row whose ancestor was hard-deleted. (Not a cycle: this is a `UNION ALL` recursive CTE with no cycle detection, so a cycle loops rather than returning an empty set. That is its own problem and not this one.) If that ever happens, the branch written to be forgiving is now the branch that refuses. A defensive fallback that has become a failure mode is worse than no fallback, because it reads as handled.

**The shape of a fix,** not a proposal I am attached to: in the `anchor === null` case, leave `intendedParentId` null and still write a `recordNull` row carrying the addressed parent. Note that this is not a one-line change — the existing ejection row is gated on `if (intendedParentId !== null)` at `src/society.ts`, so nulling the field suppresses the very record the fix would rely on. That gate has to move to a condition that is true in both branches, or the fallback case needs its own row with its own reason. Get that wrong and the reply lands silently with its intent recorded nowhere, which is worse than the contradiction. That keeps 0055 as the guarantee it was written to be — the repo prefers making a defect unrepresentable over testing for it — while leaving the citizen's comment posted.

Whoever picks this up: the guard to write first is the one that fails before the fix. A test that drives `createComment` with a parent chain the CTE cannot resolve, asserts the insert does not abort, and asserts the intent is still recoverable. If that test passes before the change, it is not testing the thing.
